title: Malteiro
summary: Malteiro is the name researchers gave to a criminal group that public reporting describes as running a malware-as-a-service operation, in which a core team maintains a banking trojan kit and affiliates rent it to run their own campaigns for a share of the proceeds. That broker model matters more than any single payload: indicators from one campaign appear in dozens of unrelated ones, so a matching file or server address proves very little about who is behind a particular infection. Reporting on this cluster concentrates on banking fraud and payment redirection in Latin America, with lures built around invoices, tax documents, and government services, and the trojan family itself is tracked publicly under the name Mispadu. Because delivery relies on ordinary email attachments and links rather than on software flaws, mail filtering and user awareness carry much of the defensive weight. Evidence lives in mail gateway records, in the download and execution chain on the endpoint, and in the fraudulent transaction patterns that the bank notices rather than the victim.

beginner.definition: Malteiro is a name for a criminal group that makes money from online banking fraud. Public reports say it sells its tools to other criminals, like a shop that rents out equipment. Buyers send fake messages that look like invoices or delivery notes. When a person opens them, a program runs that tries to steal banking details.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group shows that crime is a business with customers. One set of tools can appear in hundreds of different scams. If you only block one sender or one file, the next version arrives from a different customer. Banks and companies must watch the whole chain, from the fake message to the stolen login. Small firms are often a first step, because they hold the payment details.
howItWorks: The group builds a toolkit, a set of programs that steal banking details from a victim's computer.
It rents this toolkit to other criminals and takes a share of the stolen money.
A customer sends fake emails or messages that look like invoices or delivery notices.
The victim opens the file, and the hidden program begins to run on the computer.
The program watches the browser and copies logins, or changes the details of a payment.
The stolen information travels to a server that the group controls, and money is moved.
beginner.example: Think of a locksmith who does not rob houses himself. Instead, he sells copies of a master key and a short instruction sheet to anyone who pays. Each buyer chooses a different street and a different house. The police catch one buyer and take his key, but the locksmith simply sells more keys. Neighbours cannot protect themselves by remembering one face, because the visitors keep changing. Banking trojans spread through criminal customers in exactly this way.
takeaways: Treat unexpected invoices and delivery notices as suspicious, even from a known sender.
Confirm any change of payment details by telephone before you send money.
Report fraud attempts, because the same toolkit returns with small changes.

objectives: Explain what malware as a service means and how the affiliate model changes risk.
Describe how a banking trojan captures credentials and redirects payments.
Explain why shared indicators are weak evidence when many affiliates reuse one kit.
Identify the mail, endpoint, and banking records that support a fraud investigation.
Summarise the controls that protect payment details in a small organisation.
